title: Analytics for agencies: which tools cover which job
summary: The four analytics jobs an agency runs for every client, the tools for each, what each one misses, and how to choose when you manage many clients.
body_markdown:
Analytics for an agency is four jobs, repeated for every client: measure each site or app, report to the client, bring the data together, and keep the tracking correct. One tool rarely covers all four, so the useful question is not “which tool is best” but which job each one covers and what it leaves open. The last job is the one agencies most often leave to chance, and every report depends on it.


## The four jobs, side by side


Job Typical tools What it leaves open


Measure each client’s site or app GA4, Adobe Analytics, Amplitude, Mixpanel Whether the implementation is still sending the right data


Report to clients AgencyAnalytics, DashThis, Databox, Looker Studio Whether the numbers are right, and what they mean for the client


Bring the data together Supermetrics, Improvado, Funnel, a warehouse and a BI tool Errors at collection, which it moves along with the rest


Keep the tracking correct Manual checks in GTM and DebugView, scheduled scanners such as ObservePoint or DataTrue, real-traffic monitoring Depends on the method; manual checks don’t scale across clients


## Measure each client’s site or app


Every client already has a measurement tool, usually GA4, sometimes Adobe Analytics, Amplitude or Mixpanel next to it. For the agency the work is access and consistency: one property per client, the same events named the same way where possible, and someone who knows each setup.


What these tools don’t do is check themselves. GA4 reports what it receives, and not instantly: Google says event data appears in the Events report[up to 24 hours](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/12926615) after the event, so it is no way to check a release the day it goes live. If a release removes a parameter or a consent change drops a tag, GA4 reports the smaller number without a warning, and the client often notices first. Product tools such as Amplitude or Mixpanel add a further dependency: their analysis is only as good as the[event taxonomy](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/event-taxonomy) agreed for each client.


## Report to clients


This is the job most “agency analytics” searches are about: dashboards and reports that pull from several platforms and arrive at the client on a schedule. AgencyAnalytics, DashThis and Databox are built for it; many agencies use Looker Studio or Power BI.


A dashboard shows what the data says. Reporting tools can tell you when a connection breaks: AgencyAnalytics, for example, notifies users when an integration disconnects. That is a different thing from checking that the client’s site sent the right event with the right values. A dashboard doesn’t say whether the data is right, and it doesn’t explain what the numbers mean, which is what the client is paying for. Someone on the account team still writes that, client by client.


## Bring the data together


When a client needs data in a warehouse, or a report mixes many sources, connectors such as Supermetrics, Improvado or Funnel move it into BigQuery, Snowflake or a BI tool. They solve the plumbing.


They move whatever was collected. A purchase sent twice by the Meta Pixel arrives in the warehouse twice, cleanly joined to everything else, and a prepared dataset can’t recover tracking that was never collected.


## Keep the tracking correct


The fourth job is the one under the other three. There are three ways to do it:


- **Manual checks** in GTM Preview, the browser’s Network panel and GA4 DebugView. Precise for one site on one day; they don’t scale to a client portfolio. The[GTM debugging guide](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/gtm-debugging-guide) covers them.
- **Scheduled scanners** such as ObservePoint or DataTrue, which crawl pages and replay scripted journeys. Strong before a release; between runs, and on paths nobody scripted, nothing is watched.
- **Real-traffic monitoring** , which reads the hits real visitors send and flags what changes. It covers what visitors actually do, but a page nobody visits sends nothing to check.


The[web analytics audit](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/web-analytics-audit) explains how the three combine, and[analytics validation tools compared](https://www.trackingplan.com/blog/analytics-validation-tools-compared) puts the tools side by side.


## How Trackingplan helps agencies


When a client finds a tracking error before the agency does, the problem is no longer the tag. It is the call that follows: why didn’t you catch it? For many agencies that now use Trackingplan, that is how errors used to come to light, and every one cost a bit of the client’s trust. Nothing signals churn like a client emailing you about a broken tag.


CSA, part of Havas Media Network, describes exactly that: errors often surfaced only after clients noticed, and even when CSA hadn’t caused them, the team had to explain why they weren’t caught sooner. Today they detect and fix incidents[in less than 24 hours](https://www.trackingplan.com/customer-stories/how-csa-havas-media-network-regained-client-trust-with-out-of-the-box-data-quality-monitoring) .

## Four questions to choose your stack


1. **Who finds tracking errors today, your team or the client?** If it is the client, start here. Each time a client spots a broken conversion first, you lose some of their trust, and an account that keeps losing trust is an account at risk. A monitoring tool tells you first, so you are the one raising the flag.
2. **How long does the monthly report take your team?** If someone copies the same numbers into the same template for every client, automate that and keep the team for explaining what the numbers mean.
3. **Does any client need its data in a warehouse or a BI tool?** If so, add a connector for that client. If not, you don’t need one.
4. **How many clients does each person look after?** If every client means another login and another manual check, it won’t hold as you grow. Look for one view of all your clients.


Before you roll a tool out to every client, try it on one first: check that its numbers match the source, that a conversion means the same thing in every report, and how quickly the team would hear about a broken tag. A tool that makes reports faster without checking the data only sends wrong numbers faster.
